📌 今日核心动态
今天的研究资讯显示，人们对在线协作学习、生成式AI在教育中的应用以及儿童早期发展的研究兴趣日益浓厚。这些研究涵盖了教育技术、人工智能辅助学习、儿童认知发展等多个领域，反映出当前教育研究的多样性和创新性。

🔥 热点研究方向
1. 在线协作学习：研究者正在探索在线协作学习中的自我调节、社会共享调节等问题，发现不同的协作模式和竞争机制对学习效果有着不同的影响。对研究者的启示是，需要考虑到个体差异和群体动态来设计更有效的在线学习环境。
2. 生成式AI在教育中的应用：研究者正在研究生成式AI如何辅助教学、评估和反馈，发现其可以提高学习效率和学生的创造力，但也存在伦理问题和对传统教学方法的挑战。对研究者的启示是，需要深入探讨AI辅助教育的伦理和实施问题。
3. 儿童早期发展：研究者正在研究儿童的认知发展、语言学习和社会情感发展，发现孩子们在早期阶段就开始发展复杂的思维和社会能力。对研究者的启示是，早期教育需要更加个性化和以孩子为中心的设计。
4. 虚拟现实和游戏化学习：研究者正在探索虚拟现实和游戏化学习在教育中的应用，发现这些技术可以提高学生的参与度和学习效果，但也需要考虑到技术的局限性和伦理问题。对研究者的启示是，需要设计出更有效的虚拟现实和游戏化学习环境。

💡 值得关注的新兴方向
虚拟现实辅助的早期儿童教育是值得关注的一个新兴方向，因为它可以提供更沉浸式和交互式的学习体验，有助于提高孩子们的认知和社会情感发展。同时，生成式AI辅助的个性化教育也是一个值得跟进的方向，因为它可以根据个体差异提供更加精确和有效的学习支持。

British Journal of Educational Technolog.title: Unveiling patterns of socially shared regulation in relation to self‐regulated learning: The roles of individual profiles and group dynamics in online collaborative learning
British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  The rapid growth of massive online learning has intensified interest in self‐regulated learning (SRL) and socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL), yet empirical insights into their interplay in online collaborative learning (OCL) remain limited. This study employed a three‐layer analytical method combining cluster analysis, content analysis and complex network analysis to investigate how SSRL patterns evolve in relation to individual SRL profiles. Data from 60 undergraduates in a 16‐week course included over 16,000 trace entries (e.g. posts, replies, peer feedback) were collected and analysed. Results revealed that (1) three profiles of SRL were identified, based on learners' time investment, study regularity and help‐seeking behaviours; (2) groups with higher SSRL behavioural interaction displayed a more diverse and balanced role composition; and (3) distinct SSRL patterns emerged across SRL profiles over time. Individuals with high SRL profiles more frequently connected idea sharing with strategy using and process monitoring, while those with low SRL profiles relied on limited strategies focused mainly on idea sharing. These findings deepen the understanding of how individual regulation shapes group dynamics in online collaboration and suggest that instructional design should consider learners' SRL profiles when scaffolding their collaborative regulation processes.
                  
                    
                      
                        Practitioner Notes
                      
                      
                        What is already known about this topic
                        
                          
                            
                              Self‐regulated learning (SRL) and socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) are both essential for effective online collaborative learning (OCL), with prior research recognising their theoretical interplay.
                            
                            
                              Trace data (e.g. login frequency, timestamp and posts) offer valuable opportunities to uncover how learners engage in and coordinate regulatory behaviours throughout online collaboration.
                            
                          
                        
                      
                      
                        What this paper adds
                        
                          
                            
                              Integrating SRL profiling with mixed network analysis, this study shows how individual SRL profiles drive divergent SSRL development, highlighting shared coordination patterns and evolving interactive roles across phases.
                            
                            
                              Groups with higher SSRL interaction exhibited more diverse and balanced role composition, with central roles (e.g. leaders, animators) facilitating stronger collaborative regulation processes.
                            
                            
                              Time‐series epistemic network analysis (ENA) provides a novel analytical lens to track the evolution of SSRL patterns across collaborative phases, linking SRL profiles with group‐level regulatory dynamics.
                            
                          
                        
                      
                      
                        Implications for practice and/or policy
                        
                          
                            
                              Tailoring support to SRL profiles allows educators to offer targeted scaffolds, using prompts and planning tools for low SRL learners, while encouraging high SRL learners to lead coordination and monitoring in SSRL.
                            
                            
                              Role‐driven group design promotes collaboration structured by learners' SRL profiles.

British Journal of Educational Technolog.title: Not all collaboration benefits from competition: Collaboration modes in a computational thinking game
British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    
                    Digital game‐based learning often leverages social dynamics to enhance engagement, yet the interplay between collaborative structures and competitive pressures remains complex. This study investigated different collaboration modes and how they interact with competition to influence computational thinking (CT) learning, group metacognition and in‐game behaviours. Adopting a quasi‐experimental approach with a 3 × 2 factorial design, 148 seventh‐grade students were recruited via purposive sampling from intact classes. Participants played the game in pairs, with or without competition, in one of three collaboration modes: paired gaming on one computer, collaboration on respective computers with turn‐taking or cooperation on respective computers with role assignment. Data were analysed using quantitative methods to assess learning outcomes and behavioural sequence analysis to identify interaction patterns. Results revealed significant main effects of collaboration mode and an interaction effect between collaboration and competition. The cooperative group with competition achieved the highest CT outcomes, and the paired gaming group with competition reported the highest level of group metacognition. In contrast, the collaborative group with competition had the lowest level of learning outcomes and group metacognition. Behavioural sequence analyses identified unique patterns that corroborate the quantitative findings. Notably, competition undermined the collaborative turn‐taking mode while enhancing cooperative and paired gaming modes, highlighting the need to carefully match collaboration structures with competitive elements in designing game‐based learning.
                  
                  
                    
                    
                      
                        
                          Practitioner notes
                        
                        
                          What is already known about this topic
                          
                            
                              Collaboration and competition are widely used in digital game‐based learning (DGBL) to enhance engagement, motivation and problem‐solving.
                            
                            
                              Prior studies have often examined collaboration and competition separately, leaving the interactive effects between these social dynamics on computational thinking (CT) and group metacognition underexplored.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          What this paper adds
                          
                            
                              Different collaboration modes significantly shaped CT learning and group metacognition.
                            
                            
                              Competition alone showed no benefits for CT learning or group metacognition.
                            
                            
                              Cooperative + competition fostered clear roles, strategic play and higher CT.
                            
                            
                              Competition weakened collaboration learning's CT performance and led to fragmented behaviours.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          Implications for practice and policy
                          
                            
                              Carefully match collaboration structures with competition features when designing game‐based or group learning activities.
                            
                            
                              Use competition selectively—beneficial in cooperative tasks with clear role assignments, but potentially detrimental in open collaboration requiring trust and mutual regulation.
                            
                            
                              Integrate competitive and collaborative elements intentionally rather than additively.

British Journal of Educational Technolog.title:
Hybrid intelligence feedback systems in design thinking development: Stage‐specific insights on pedagogical effects and characteristics of generative
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    and instructors
British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  Fostering design thinking relies on instructional feedback, yet traditional instructor‐led methods face practical limitations. Although generative AI (GenAI) may offer promising solutions based on its advantages, existing studies predominantly characterise it as a performance‐enhancing task assistant rather than as a feedback‐providing pedagogical agent for the intrinsic growth of design thinking. The study compares the pedagogical effects on students' design thinking and students' perceptions of feedback systems by GenAI and human instructors. A within‐class randomised experimental design was conducted with 80 undergraduates. Results indicate no significant overall difference in learning gains, but reveal respective stage‐specific strengths: GenAI proved more effective during the ‘empathise’ stage, associated with superior timeliness and privacy, while human instructors excelled in the ‘prototype’ stage, valued for their contextual anchoring. Comparable effects yet complementary functions were observed in other stages, reinforcing GenAI's augmentative role instead of substitution. Findings collectively demonstrate that the effectiveness and strengths of feedback systems are not static and uniform but dynamically aligned with the learning demands across educational settings. Practical insights for designing hybrid intelligence feedback systems and theoretical implications were finally discussed.
                  
                    
                      
                        Practitioner notes
                      
                      
                        What is already known about this topic
                        
                          
                            
                              Instructional feedback is crucial for fostering design thinking; however, traditional instructor‐led feedback is often constrained by issues of scalability, timeliness and consistency.
                            
                            
                              Generative AI (GenAI) shows promise to serve as an additional feedback agent, but its role has been explored more as a performance‐enhancing task assistant rather than a feedback‐providing pedagogical agent for the intrinsic growth of design thinking.
                            
                          
                        
                      
                      
                        What this paper adds
                        
                          
                            
                              The study demonstrates that GenAI leads to greater learning gains in the ‘empathise’ stage, while human instructors are more effective in the ‘prototype’ stage.
                            
                            
                              The study underscores their comparable effect while serving distinct and complementary roles at ‘define’, ‘ideate’ and ‘reflect’ stages.
                            
                            
                              The study highlights their respective stage‐specific strengths and associates them with learning gains across the design thinking process.
                            
                            
                              The study provides practical insights for designing hybrid feedback systems that strategically orchestrate GenAI and human instructors to maximise pedagogical impact.
                            
                          
                        
                      
                      
                        Implications for practice and/or policy
                        
                          
                            
                              Educational policy should promote the design of hybrid feedback systems that strategically align the inherent characteristics of different feedback agents with the stage‐specific learning demands across various educational contexts.
                            
                            
                              Curriculum development should emphasise building students' relevant competencies (e.g., feedback literacy, AI competency, etc.), equipping them to seek, evaluate and synthesise input from multiple agents effectively.

Educational Technology Research and Deve.title: Game-based learning for ethics: benefits, challenges, and dilemmas
Educational Technology Research and Deve.abstract:
Abstract
                  Ethics is recognized as a foundational element of human decision-making and a critical competency across educational disciplines, especially in STEM, where solving authentic, complex problems is essential. Traditional methods of ethics instruction often fail to provide the engagement needed for learners to grasp abstract ethical challenges. In contrast, game-based learning offers an experiential approach capable of supporting ethical literacy. Yet, despite their potential, games may also hinder learning or even promote unethical behavior, highlighting a critical but often overlooked challenge: balancing engaging gameplay with the meaningful integration of ethics-related objectives. Given the growing popularity and accessibility of analogue games in ethics education, this study explores their potential through four business ethics board games, each featuring distinct ethical goals, mechanics, and themes. A four-day workshop was conducted with 32 adult participants from diverse cultural, professional, and age backgrounds, with structured interviews following each gameplay session. By thematically analyzing participants’ experiences and perceptions, the study aims to deepen understanding of the complex interplay between games and ethics learning. Adopting a dialectical perspective, the research critically explores both the benefits and challenges of game-based approaches across different stages of the learning process. As a result, the pedagogical dilemmas related to rules, social modes, identity framing, systems nudging, personalized design, and ethics positioning were identified and discussed, spanning personal, behavioral, and environmental dimensions. Building on these insights, recommendations are proposed for designing and implementing games in ethics education, addressing aspects such as facilitation, instructions, goal settings, and social dynamics, thereby supporting meaningful, ethically informed learning experiences.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title:
Students and Instructors' Perceptions of Integrating Generative
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    in Assessment Within the Context of the
                    <scp>UAE</scp>
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming assessment practices in higher education, offering opportunities for efficiency and personalization while raising concerns related to academic integrity, fairness, and responsible use. Understanding how different users perceive and engage with GenAI is essential, particularly within rapidly advancing digital contexts such as the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
                  
                  
                    Objectives
                    This study investigates students' and instructors' perceptions of GenAI integration in assessment and examines the relationships among perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, perceived risk, attitudes, and responsible use, including the moderating role of user type.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    An explanatory sequential mixed‐methods design was employed. Quantitative data were collected from 193 participants (163 students and 30 instructors) using a validated survey instrument. Correlation, regression, mediation, and moderation analyses were conducted, complemented by qualitative thematic analysis of open‐ended responses.
                  
                  
                    Results
                    Findings revealed significant positive relationships among all constructs. Perceived usefulness and ease of use were combined into a higher‐order Technology Acceptance Model construct that strongly predicted attitudes. Perceived risk significantly influenced both attitudes and responsible use, emerging as the strongest predictor of responsible behaviour. Attitude partially mediated the relationship between technology acceptance and responsible use. User role significantly moderated this relationship, with a stronger effect observed among instructors. Qualitative findings indicated generally positive but cautious attitudes, highlighting concerns about over‐reliance, accuracy, and academic integrity, alongside a continued intention to use GenAI.
                  
                  
                    Conclusions
                    GenAI adoption in assessment is shaped by a balance between perceived benefits and risk awareness. The findings highlight the importance of promoting responsible use through clear policies, training, and assessment design, offering practical implications for integrating GenAI within higher education systems.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title:
The Effects of K‐12 Artificial Intelligence Education in Enhancing
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    Literacy: A Meta‐Analysis
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    The initiation of K‐12 artificial intelligence education has been led by numerous governments and institutions. However, most existing meta‐analyses have focused on the effectiveness of AI tools for learning support (AI in education; AIED), rather than AI education, and research on comprehensive evidence on how AI education improves learners' AI literacy remains limited.
                  
                  
                    Objectives
                    This meta‐analysis aims to provide an additional understanding of the future direction of K‐12 AI education by synthesising and analysing existing interventions in AI education classes to enhance learners' AI literacy and holistically discussing their effectiveness.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    A total of 16 source articles were searched and analysed from 8 databases, considering our inclusion and exclusion criteria, yielding 57 effect sizes. These effect sizes were used to examine the effectiveness of various K‐12 AI education classes in enhancing AI literacy.
                  
                  
                    Results and Conclusion
                    
                      The analysis showed a significant overall mean effect of AI education classes (
                      g
                       = 0.892, CI: [0.548, 1.236],
                      p
                       < 0.001) on enhancing AI literacy. Moreover, moderator analyses by publication type, year of publication, and school level of the participants did not reveal any significant patterns, indicating that K‐12 AI education classes exhibit consistently positive effects across different contexts. The findings underscore the importance of continued research on K‐12 AI education and offer a strong rationale for its ongoing integration by policymakers across various governments. To support discussion on this topic, future studies can reference this research and investigate the topic with more published articles.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title:
Teacher Mediation and the Contingent Promise of Generative
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    in Mathematics Education
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    The integration of generative AI (GenAI) into education, specifically into teaching and learning, offers potential for personalised learning, but at the same time, it poses a challenge to whether it fosters student agency. Moreover, it also threatens to exacerbate entrenched inequalities, which have the potential to create new barriers for most of the learners. A gap exists in understanding how GenAI can be rethought as a dynamic scaffold that promotes cognitive struggle for conceptual understanding while actively advancing equitable participation.
                  
                  
                    Objective
                    The study aims to critically analyse how secondary school mathematics teachers implement GenAI for adaptive scaffolding. Moreover, this study aims to investigate the pedagogical and ethical tensions, particularly concerning equity and power dynamics, that emerge from using GenAI during classroom interactions.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    
                      This study employed a qualitative research design. Data were collected over an eight‐week intervention, which included in‐depth teacher interviews (
                      n
                       = 10), student focus groups (
                      n
                       = 24), and classroom observations in two public secondary schools purposively selected for their contrasting socioeconomic and technology integration profiles.
                    
                  
                  
                    Results
                    Based on the results and findings, five distinct teacher‐mediated GenAI scaffolding practices that support equitable knowledge construction were identified. Findings indicate that strategies such as prompting for problem formulation through AI‐generated inquiry and facilitating critical comparison of AI‐generated outputs were associated with deeper student engagement and reasoning within the conditions of this study, particularly when teachers exercised intentional critical mediation. Conversely, unmediated use of GenAI amplified significant challenges, such as a redistribution of epistemic authority, a tangible “algorithmic divide” in AI performance between well‐resourced and under‐resourced schools, and risks due to the absence of how data should be handled. The technology consistently amplified existing pedagogical conditions, which are both effective and inequitable.
                  
                  
                    Conclusion
                    The promise of GenAI is strictly contingent on a commitment to equity. This means that its outcomes are determined not by the GenAI itself but by pedagogical intentionality and systemic support. Unexamined adoption poses risks that worsen disparities for marginalised students and reinforces passive learning. Thus, by proposing a framework for equitable integration centred on the teacher's role as a critical mediator, this expertise serves as a model for sustainable pedagogical practice in the digital age.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title:
The Impact of
                    <scp>ChatGPT</scp>
                    on Higher Education: A Systematic Review of Global Opportunities, Perceptions, and Challenges
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) has fundamentally changed how education is delivered and how students perform. Since its launch, ChatGPT, a popular generative AI tool, has generated mixed reactions.
                  
                  
                    Objectives
                    This research systematically reviews the opportunities, perceptions, and challenges of using ChatGPT among faculty members and students at higher education levels. Our review identified key themes and patterns in the literature and provided a comprehensive understanding of the different opinions held by students and faculty.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    We included peer‐reviewed journal articles and conference papers published between January 1, 2022 and October 20, 2025, sourced from APA PsycInfo, CINAHL Ultimate, Education Source Ultimate, ERIC and Web of Science. From 1046 initial records, 58 articles met the inclusion criteria. We also conducted a targeted search on December 10, 2024, which identified 12 additional studies from Google Scholar (6) and Consensus App (6). We then performed a final search on October 20, 2025, using the Consensus App, resulting in 12 more recent studies, bringing the total to 82 articles. Thematic content analysis and descriptive statistics identified key themes and patterns across the literature.
                  
                  
                    Results and Conclusion
                    Our review showed that faculty members and students hold differing opinions regarding ChatGPT's accuracy, reliability, and ethical implications, as well as its future role in higher education. Some view ChatGPT as a valuable tool for teaching and learning, while others remain sceptical. We conclude that appropriate measures should be taken to ensure that ChatGPT is used responsibly and equitably in higher education.

Education and Information Technologies.title: When university students’ insecurities drive them to rely excessively on Artificial Intelligence: Relationship between fear of failure, self-esteem, social support and ChatGPT dependence
Education and Information Technologies.abstract:
Abstract
                  In learning processes, students with a high fear of failure and low self-esteem may be more inclined to use technologies like artificial intelligence (ChatGPT…) to avoid making mistakes, potentially even developing a dependency on such tools. However, it is believed that having peers and teachers who help these students build confidence and receive support to overcome failure could act as a buffer against attachment to technological tools like ChatGPT. To test this hypothesis, 467 university students participated by completing a series of scales to measure their fear of failure, self-esteem, peer support, teacher support, and dependency on ChatGPT. Following a moderated mediation analysis, the results revealed that the initial hypothesis was not supported. Indeed, higher levels of fear of failure and lower levels of self-esteem did not lead to an increase in ChatGPT dependence. Likewise, social support from peers and teachers did not influence the previously mentioned relationship.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: Generative Scaffolding in Pre-Trip Games: Effects of a GenAI-Chatbot on Inquiry-Based Learning
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract: To address the issue of “travel without learning” in study tours caused by insufficient preparation, digital game-based learning (DGBL) serves as an engaging pre-trip solution. However, traditional DGBL’s static feedback limits open-ended inquiry and personalized learning. To overcome this, we proposed the DGBL-GAI approach to provide dynamic scaffolding, and developed a “Field Trip Preparatory Game” as its specific application. A preliminary quasi-experiment involved 83 seventh-grade students: the experimental group (n = 41) used the game guided by the DGBL-GAI approach, while the control group (n = 42) received traditional script-based static prompts. Results indicated that the DGBL-GAI approach was associated with better learning achievement and self-efficacy. Furthermore, an exploratory subgroup analysis based on post-intervention self-efficacy suggested a preliminary association: the achievement advantage of the DGBL-GAI approach appeared more evident among students with lower self-efficacy. Finally, behavioral pattern analysis provided supportive process-level evidence suggesting that, within the current sample, the experimental group appeared to engage in a more proactive and strategic learning pattern, using AI as an information integration hub and showing greater persistence, whereas the control group followed a more linear and passive learning pathway.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: From Simulation to Dialogue: A Quasi-Experimental Mixed-Methods Study of Conversational-AI Supported VR Fire Escape Training
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract:
Virtual reality fire escape drills can support procedural learning. However, many implementations rely on scripted interaction that limits learner-initiated inquiry during evacuation. In this study, a Conversational AI Supported VR Fire Escape System (
                    CAVR)
                    was developed as a Unity based virtual reality drill integrated with the Live Character API through Web Real-Time Communication (WebRTC) for low-latency speech interaction and with retrieval augmented generation grounded in a curated fire safety knowledge base. A quasi-experimental mixed methods design was applied with 163 first year undergraduates from two universities. The experimental group used the
                    CAVR
                    System and the control group used a virtual reality fire escape system without conversational support. Results indicated higher post test knowledge achievement in the experimental group after adjustment for pre-test scores with a significant group effect. Higher behavioral intentions were observed across dimensions with small to medium effect sizes. Trust levels were substantially higher in the experimental group with a large effect size. Interview themes indicated that learner-initiated inquiry during embodied action continuous dialog verification through persistent subtitles and perceived grounding of guidance through retrieval augmented generation contributed to the observed outcome pattern. The implications of using a
                    CAVR
                    System for fire safety education are discussed.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: Unveiling the Cognitive and Affective Mechanisms of Virtual Museum Learning: A Partial Least Squares Analysis
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract: Virtual museums, as important carriers of immersive learning environments, are changing traditional knowledge acquisition and cultural inheritance methods. However, existing research focuses on direct relationships between virtual museum design features and learning outcomes, lacking systematic revelation of cognitive and affective mechanism pathways in the learning process. Therefore, this study constructs a Cognitive-Affective Model of Virtual Museum Learning (CAMVML), aiming to reveal complex relationships among virtual museums’ technological features, learners’ cognitive and affective experiences, and learning outcomes. This study involved 254 seventh-grade students as participants, utilized structured questionnaires for data collection, and employed partial least squares structural equation modeling to empirically validate the proposed model. Results showed that the virtual museum’s interactivity and autonomy, learners’ germane cognitive load, flow experience, and situational interest significantly and positively predicted learning outcomes. Additionally, germane cognitive load and flow experience played important mediating roles between technical features and learning outcomes. Results verified multiple hypothesized paths in the proposed model and highlighted the necessity of synergy between cognitive and affective factors in virtual learning environments. This study provides a structured theoretical framework for understanding cognitive and affective mechanisms of virtual museum learning and provides empirical support for instructional design and practical application of immersive learning environments.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: Complementary Tools or Competitors? ChatGPT-Generated and Peer-Delivered Formative Feedback in EFL Writing Classes: Effectiveness, Perceptions, and Recommendations
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract:
There has been growing interest in EFL writing classrooms regarding the use of ChatGPT for giving feedback. Peer-delivered feedback, long celebrated for its collaborative and motivational advantages, now coexists with ChatGPT’s promise of instant, technically precise corrections. This mixed-methods study, designed as a convergent parallel design, tracked 48 Turkish university EFL learners across a semester, analyzing eight writing tasks reviewed by both peers and ChatGPT, alongside student reflections from structured written interviews. The results revealed that peer feedback excelled in nurturing coherence, structure, and idea development, while ChatGPT-generated feedback proved stronger for grammar and vocabulary corrections. Participants appreciated ChatGPT’s speed and objectivity but perceived it as tone-deaf to cultural nuance and rhetorical purpose. Although peer-delivered feedback was regarded as occasionally inconsistent, it provided authentic engagement and a sense of audience. Building on these converging findings, this study offers a reasoned pedagogical implication, rather than an empirically tested model, termed
                    feedback sequencing
                    : using ChatGPT first for technical cleanup, then peers for higher-order concerns such as clarity and impact. This staged proposal, which warrants direct experimental verification in future research, is theoretically grounded in cognitive load theory and sociocognitive perspectives on formative feedback. The findings urge educators to weave AI literacy into curricula, not as a replacement for peer interaction, but as a complement that preserves the irreplaceable human dimensions of learning to write.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: How Undergraduate and Graduate Students Self-Regulate GenAI Use in Project-Based Learning: Choosing, Creating, Filtering, and Stopping Strategies
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract:
Generative AI (GenAI) is now common in university project work, yet previous studies often examine students’ trust, creativity, overload, or engagement separately. This leaves a key gap: how students regulate GenAI across a full project workflow. This exploratory study addresses that gap by examining a four-process “
                    AI-mediated Self-Regulated Learning
                    ” (
                    AI-SRL
                    ) cycle: (1) evaluating and selecting GenAI suggestions, (2) experiencing shifts in creative agency, (3) managing overload through filtering and summarizing, and (4) monitoring time and energy to stop or continue working with GenAI. We conducted a two-course basic qualitative design study with 97 undergraduate and graduate students. Data came from an open-ended questionnaire aligned to the four processes. We used inductive content analysis with a shared codebook, reliability checks, and cross-level comparisons. Findings show that students use combinations of strategies across the
                    AI-SRL
                    cycle. They exercise agency through goal alignment, revision, and verification, with graduates reporting stronger cross-checking and source-based justification. Creativity was described as a conditional outcome: it increased when GenAI widened ideas but declined when it replaced personal exploration. Overload was managed through targeted prompts and structured outputs, again more common among graduates. Most students did not lose track of time; they used clear stopping cues such as fatigue, repetition, or satisfaction. Together, results reveal two distinct metacognitive regulation styles: “
                    Exploratory-Simplification
                    ” and “
                    Systematic-Methodical
                    ”.

Early Childhood Education Journal.title: “But how does flying work on gravity when you just go up?”: An Investigation of Children’s Science Questions While Reading Life and Physical Science Books in Early Childhood
Early Childhood Education Journal.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Children’s question-asking during early childhood plays a central role in cognitive development, reflecting children’s natural curiosity about the world. While research on early science learning has focused on informal contexts (e.g., home) where adults play a key role, less is known about children’s own contributions during these interactions, particularly across different science domains. Our study investigated how children aged 4 to 7 years engage in scientific inquiry by comparing the types of questions children asked while reading a life science book and a physical science book. We recorded 93 mother–child dyads reading two science books from the popular
                    Let’s-Read-and-Find-Out-Science
                    series. Transcribed utterances were coded for five types of science questions. Repeated-measures ANOVAs revealed that children asked more science-related questions during the physical science book than the life science book, with explanation- and fact-seeking questions being the most prevalent within both books. Science question-asking increased from ages four to five but stabilized around age six. No average gender differences in question-asking were observed. Bivariate correlations showed that children’s science questions correlated positively with time spent reading and parents’ overall science talk across both books. These findings challenge assumptions that young children are developmentally unready or uninterested in science—especially physical science. By centering on children’s questions, our study highlights everyday experiences, such as shared book reading, can serve as contexts that support children’s engagement in scientific inquiry during early childhood.

Early Childhood Education Journal.title: Writing Identity and Self-Efficacy in Early Childhood Across Home and School Contexts
Early Childhood Education Journal.abstract:
Abstract
                  Early writing development involves more than acquiring transcriptional skills; it is closely bound up with the emergence of children's identities as writers and their beliefs in their own capacity to write. Drawing on sociocultural theory and social cognitive theory, this study examined how young children construct writing self-efficacy and writer identity in relation to how parents and educators define and recognize early writing. A convergent mixed-methods design was used to triangulate data from 245 four-year-old children, 87 educators, and 156 parents in public preschool settings in Greece. Semi-structured interviews with children, supported by visual prompts depicting five developmental writing stages (drawing, scribbling, letter strings, invented spelling, and conventional spelling), were paired with parallel educator and parent surveys assessing recognition of, and rationales for, writing at each stage. Descriptive quantitative analysis was used to identify patterns of recognition across developmental stages, and qualitative content analysis was used to explore the rationales underlying these recognition patterns. Findings revealed a developmentally progressive convergence between children's self-perceptions and adults' recognition of their writing: agreement with educators was strongest at the earliest stages (drawing and scribbling), whereas agreement with parents emerged mainly at more conventional stages, with the highest convergence found for invented and conventional spelling. Children's self-identification as writers was strongest when their earliest writing attempts were validated by educators and the broader social environment. These findings suggest that writer identity and self-efficacy in early childhood are shaped not only by children's own developing skills but by the extent to which the adults around them recognize early, non-conventional marks as legitimate writing, underscoring the need for greater alignment between home and school conceptions of what counts as writing.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: The nano-field: Theorising ethical tensions at the intersection of institutional rules and child-centred research
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: Early childhood research increasingly foregrounds children’s participation and complex agency, yet ethical tensions persist when child-centred research unfolds within adult-governed pedagogic institutions. These tensions often arise in fleeting interactional moments where participation redistributes authority and unsettles institutional norms and peer hierarchies. Drawing on data collected in 2016 with 18 children aged 3–5 across two London nurseries, this paper analyses two research encounters involving peer conflict and exclusion. The findings demonstrate that research participation can recalibrate symbolic capital within pedagogic settings, enabling children to negotiate, stretch, and at times subvert institutional rules in real time. These moments are ethically intensified because the researcher’s positioning simultaneously softens and reconfigures adult authority. To theorise this hyper-local dynamic, I introduce the concept of the nano-field; a nested research field within broader pedagogic and institutional fields where capital, hierarchy, and rules are renegotiated. In dialogue with my earlier work on agile agency, the nano-field specifies how children discern rules through situated co-reflexivity, embody research identities, and reconfigure peer hierarchies. The paper concludes that without theorising the research encounter itself as a nested field, ethical dilemmas risk being reduced either to procedural ethics or to celebratory accounts of agency. The nano-field therefore constitutes a necessary refinement of field theory and offers a framework for ethically responsive child-centred research in early childhood settings.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: Children’s use of symbolic “anchors”: Color and shape in map-making activities
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: This research study focuses on children’s symbolic development, especially looking at color and shape as symbolic anchors in children’s expressive communication. Framed by Vygotsky’s cognitive development theory, which includes the roles of social interaction, cultural tools, and the zone of proximal development (ZPD), as well as Mead’s social interactionism, the study was designed as mixed-methods research with data collection from children’s map artifacts, map-making video recording and audio transcriptions, and a data collection matrix. By tracking the performance of 10 children (n/x = 10) in creating maps for 2 years, when they were approximately 4 years old (year 1, mean age = 52.5 months), and in Pre-K (year 2, mean age = 71 months), when they were approximately 5 years old, we examined children’s symbol use. It was observed that exposure to and engagement with relational language promotes children’s analogical reasoning. We also found that the children’s use of symbols, and especially symbolic anchors, increased overtime, demonstrating expanded perspective-taking ability. Lastly, it is our observation that children’s use of shape as a symbolic anchor seems to appear prior to children’s use of color in the emergence of symbolic representation.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: Material-discursive dimensions of early narrative learning in a kindergarten classroom
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: This study applies posthuman theory and materiality to early literacy learning to support shifts in school-based practices from human-centered, developmental models using scripted curricula to one that acknowledges literacy as an intra-active, material-discursive process. The research was conducted in a kindergarten public school classroom where, twice per week, children listened to read alouds and crafted narratives using paper-based and digital tools. The intra-actions recognized children, books, recordings, and writing tools as active participants in the learning process. Learning was entangled with children’s bodies, voices, emotions, and memories. The material-discursive engagements altered the children’s becomings as literate beings. The findings challenge a narrow view of literacy and the child as the sole agent of literacy, highlighting how objects, gestures, playfulness, and cultural stories intra-act to shape learning. The study reimagines storytelling as a dynamic, embodied, and relational practice that disrupts conventional literacy pedagogies.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: Researching Lx English among young children: Challenges and complexities
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: Most research on Lx English has focused on adolescent and adult learners, despite growing evidence that young children encounter and use English well before formal instruction begins. Studies specifically addressing the use of and exposure to Lx English among young children, ages 3–7 in Sweden and similar countries remain scarce. This paper addresses that gap by critically examining the methodological and ethical complexities involved in researching young children’s exposure to and use of English as an additional language in Swedish preschools. Given the critical importance of language development in early childhood, it is essential to investigate how children engage with and experience language through diverse modalities. This paper aims to critically discuss the challenges and complexities encountered in the research on young children’s exposure to English as an additional language (Lx) in Swedish preschools. In particular, the study investigates how different methodological approaches can capture the multifaceted, context-dependent, and often informal nature of Lx English in early childhood settings. The methodological framework includes observations, field notes, interviews with children and preschool teachers, questionnaires, and age-relevant language proficiency tests. The study is conducted across four distinct Swedish preschool contexts. Rather than presenting detailed empirical findings, this paper focuses on methodological and ethical reflections emerging from the study, highlighting the complexities and challenges inherent in conducting research with young children in such settings. The discussion addresses key issues that may prove significant for researchers engaged in preschool research, particularly how different methods can help amplify children's voices. The paper concludes with practical implications for researchers in the field of early childhood education and care, emphasizing the importance of adopting a child-centered perspective when children are the primary focus of research.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: Flexibility or fragility? Ambivalences of temporary agency work in German Early Childhood Education and Care
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: Temporary agency work has become a growing yet ambivalent feature of Germany’s Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC) system. Though agency staff make up only a small portion of the workforce, their presence reveals core weaknesses in the sector—persistent staff shortages, rigid employment models, and limited career perspectives. Drawing on a qualitative, multi-perspective study involving agency workers, agency executives, and ECEC managers, this article analyses the structural and professional ambivalences of agency employment. It situates these experiences within debates on professionalisation, individualisation, and workforce policy. The findings highlight four recurring tensions: flexibility versus insecurity, relief versus loss of belonging, financial incentives versus inequality, and autonomy versus dependency. These contradictions illuminate how agency work stabilises institutions while simultaneously eroding professional continuity. The article concludes that the attractiveness of agency work exposes deficits in permanent employment structures. Incorporating elements such as flexible scheduling, reduced administrative burdens, and rotational experiences into stable contracts could strengthen workforce sustainability and pedagogical quality in ECEC.
